instruction_given_to_self: SEPARATE authoring pass, explicit spurious mindset. Reading the same updated 60-row slice, name 10 features that are plausibly PREDICTIVE but NOT quality. Round 1 already declared: applied-domain framing, abstract length, branded method name, enumerated formatting, LaTeX residue, resource magnitude, superlative density, dominant topic, benchmark name-dropping, anonymised-repo boilerplate, industrial compute. Round 2 must therefore target channels round 1 left UNTESTED. Label-blind: `judgement` was never loaded; no criterion references acceptance or any outcome.
scale: 0-10 integer, NA if the abstract gives no evidence bearing on the criterion

criteria.name: Inline author-year citations inside the abstract
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 by how much the abstract cites prior work inline in author-year form (for example 'Smith et al., 2019') rather than referring to prior work in prose without citations. Score the citation practice only, not whether the citations are apt.
criteria.rationale: Untested in round 1 and highly visible here: R2-DH02 '(Anil et al., 2021)', R2-DH09 '(LeCun et al.,1990; Hassibi et al., 1993)' and '(Lee et al. (2018))', R2-DH14 '(Manning et. al, 2020)' and '(Warstadt & Bowman, 2020)'. Whether an abstract carries citations at all is a subfield and submission-era convention, not a property of the work.

criteria.name: First-person narrative density
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 by how heavily the abstract is written in the first person plural — 'we propose', 'we show', 'we find', 'our method' — as opposed to impersonal or passive construction. Count the register only.
criteria.rationale: Pure writing-register channel, orthogonal to round-1 B07 (superlatives). R2-DH20 and R2-DH29 are dense with 'we show / we propose / our analysis'; R2-DL52 and R2-DL45 lean impersonal. Person and voice conventions travel with subfield and author training.

criteria.name: Syntactic complexity independent of total length
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how long and multi-clausal the abstract's individual SENTENCES are — subordinate clauses, parentheticals, chains of qualifiers — judged independently of how long the abstract is overall. A short abstract of tangled sentences scores high; a long abstract of short sentences scores low.
criteria.rationale: Round-1 B02 measured total length and was the strongest single nuisance (.567). This deliberately separates sentence-level complexity from total extent, so the round-2 discount can tell the two apart. R2-DH11 and R2-DL54 are heavily subordinated; R2-DH07 and R2-DL30 are short-sentenced.

criteria.name: Typographic emphasis used inside the abstract
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses typographic emphasis to direct attention — bold, italics, or emphasis markup around names, numbers, or claims. Score the emphasis practice only, regardless of what is emphasised.
criteria.rationale: Untested in round 1, which covered raw LaTeX residue (B04) but not deliberate emphasis. R2-DL34 bolds 'beats average human performance' and '18.6\% to 81.7\%' and '340\% relative increase'; R2-DL12 bolds FashionMT and MAI; R2-DH01 and R2-DL44 use \emph{} throughout. A house-style artefact.

criteria.name: Rhetorical questions posed in the abstract
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract uses questions as a rhetorical device to frame its contribution ('Can a machine ...?', 'How can we ...?', 'This raises the question: ...'). Score the device only.
criteria.rationale: Untested channel, clearly present: R2-DL36 ('Can a machine learn machine learning?'), R2-DL35 ('How can we use implicit human feedback to accelerate ...?'), R2-DL46 ('can these existing research efforts actually effectively achieve ...?'), R2-DH22 ('how can we design a unified search space ...'). A framing mannerism.

criteria.name: Non-idiomatic English and grammatical slips
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract departs from fluent idiomatic English — agreement errors, article misuse, awkward collocations, malformed constructions. Score surface fluency only, not the clarity of the underlying ideas.
criteria.rationale: Untested and deliberately included as the round's hardest audit case, because fluency is arguably quality-adjacent: if the blind auditor routes it to the bank, that is an informative disagreement rather than a failure. Visible instances: R2-DH19 ('we keenly aware of numerous unsaturated in-channel weights'), R2-DL27 ('is proposed to effectively tackles these generated video quality problems'), R2-DL46 ('this thus inevitably raise a critical research question'). Fluency tracks author first-language, an institutional attribute.

criteria.name: Acronym density
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 by how many distinct capitalised abbreviations the abstract introduces or uses per unit of text, counting field-standard acronyms as well as newly coined ones. Score density only.
criteria.rationale: Distinct from round-1 B06, which scored whether the METHOD is branded; this counts total acronym load including inherited field vocabulary. R2-DL37 (SSPINNpose, IMU), R2-DL34 (MCTS, DPO, LLM), R2-DL51 (BDL, KL, ifBDL) versus the acronym-light R2-DH00 and R2-DH13. Notation load is a subfield convention.

criteria.name: Explicit priority or first-ness claims
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how prominently the abstract asserts priority — 'to the best of our knowledge, the first', 'for the first time', 'we present the first study of'. Score the assertion of priority only, not whether it is true or whether the work is novel.
criteria.rationale: Untested rhetorical positioning move, common in this slice: R2-DL30 ('to the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that bridges pruning with the theory of differential privacy'), R2-DH22 ('we study the problem of automated graph Transformer, for the first time'), R2-DL46 ('we thus perform the first measurement study'). Priority rhetoric is a submission convention distinct from actual novelty, which the bank already scores at 79/88.

criteria.name: Membership in the privacy / security / adversarial-robustness subfield
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how far the abstract belongs to the privacy, security, adversarial-robustness, or attack-and-defence cluster of machine learning. Score topic membership only; work of any quality in any other subfield scores 0.
criteria.rationale: A finer-grained topic marker than round-1 B05 (which scored the dominant LLM/diffusion topics). This cluster is conspicuous on the dense-low side of the round-2 slice: R2-DL30 (pruning and differential privacy), R2-DL31 (DP-SGD), R2-DL43 (membership inference), R2-DL45 (adversarial vulnerability with categorical input), R2-DL46 (object-hiding attacks) — while R2-DH00 is also adversarial, which makes the channel a real test rather than a giveaway.

criteria.name: Hedging-word density
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how heavily the abstract hedges — 'may', 'might', 'could', 'suggests', 'potential', 'appears to', 'we believe'. Count the hedging register only, not whether the hedging is warranted.
criteria.rationale: The opposite pole from round-1 B07 (superlative density) and untested. The V block carries a v_kw_hedge keyword count, so a judged version lets the two registers be discounted on the same footing. R2-DH00 ('we believe that ...', 'in a certain sense'), R2-DH24 ('suggest that MQL compares favorably') versus the hedge-free R2-DL43 and R2-DL57.
